blocks.text: Dear Mr. Villegas:

This letter sets down the terms on which our firm will advise {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} on the automation of its back-office operations, and it becomes our agreement at the moment you countersign the enclosed copy and return it to me. I have written it out at some length and in plain terms, in the belief that an engagement of this kind proceeds more surely when both sides have read one account of it before any work is begun, and that the understanding reached now, on paper, is worth a good deal more than the goodwill we would otherwise be left to fall back on later. I would ask you to weigh what follows against your own sense of the assignment, and to tell me of any point on which the two do not sit easily together before you put your name to it.
The Work We Have Agreed to Undertake

The assignment is the automation of the routine, high-volume work that runs through the finance and administrative back office at {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}}: the invoice handling, the account reconciliations, the recurring closing tasks, and the reports that at present consume more of your people's time than the judgment they actually contain would warrant. We will begin by setting down a faithful account of how that work is done today, following each process from the point at which it starts to the point at which it ends, marking the places where a task is carried by a person only because it always has been, and separating the steps that genuinely call for judgment from those that a rule could carry as well or better. From that account we will identify the processes whose automation would repay the effort soonest, set out how each of them might be redesigned, and work alongside your team toward a sequence of changes it is able to adopt and to maintain once we have gone. Where a candidate for automation carries a cost or a risk alongside its saving, we will say so plainly rather than present the saving on its own.

It is worth being equally clear about where the work stops. This is a diagnosis of how {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} runs its back office and a design for automating the parts of it that should be automated; it is neither the building and installation of the software that would carry those designs nor a reduction of your staff, both of which remain yours to decide and to lead unless we later agree, in writing, a separate engagement covering them. Should the scope need to change once we are under way, whether because you ask it or because the work brings to light something that neither of us can yet foresee, we will describe the change and settle its terms with you before we act on it.
The People Who Will Carry It

I will hold this engagement for the firm and answer for what we deliver under it, while the day-to-day work is carried by two of our research associates. Pamela Miller will run the examination of your current processes and the checking of every figure and claim on which the design comes to rest, so that nothing we put in front of you leans on a number we have not traced back to its source. Matthew Parrish will assemble the outside reference points, the measures of how comparable finance functions are run and at what cost, against which we can judge whether a given process at {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} is handled well or merely handled as it always has been. You will work with a small and settled team, and the people whose names stand on our analysis will be the people who have done it.
Fees and Payment

Our fee for this engagement is a fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2021-001.fee}}, which covers the work described above together with the meetings, correspondence, and interim materials that ordinarily accompany it, and which does not extend to work we might later agree to add, such as the building or installation of the automation itself, that we would scope and price with you separately before beginning. We will render invoices against the fee at regular intervals as the work proceeds, and each invoice falls due within thirty days of its date. I have set the figure here, in the body of the letter, so that you are able to weigh it directly against the work it is meant to buy.
Term and Termination

The engagement will commence on {{fact:f:E-2021-001.start}} and is scoped to run for approximately four months, that being the period over which we have planned the diagnosis and the design work, though I will tell you early if the assignment proves to want more time than that or less. Either of us may bring it to an end on reasonable written notice to the other. Should you choose to end it, you will owe our fee earned to the date of termination together with any costs properly incurred to that point and nothing beyond; should we do so, which we would undertake only for a reason our professional standards require of us, we will return any part of the fee that answers to work not yet performed and will help hand the assignment over in an orderly way.
Confidentiality

We will treat the information you place in our hands, together with the fact and the substance of this engagement, as confidential, and we will use what you disclose to us solely for the work you have retained us to perform. We ask the same of {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} in respect of the methods and materials we bring to the assignment. These obligations will outlast the completion or the termination of the engagement, and neither of us will disclose the other's confidential information except so far as the law or a proper regulatory authority compels, and then, where we are able, on notice to the other.
Limitation of Liability

We will perform this engagement with the care and skill our profession expects, and our advice will represent our considered judgment on the information available to us. We do not, however, warrant a particular commercial result, since the time and cost that automation can save depend in large part on decisions and actions that will lie with your organization once the design is in its hands rather than with ours. Our aggregate liability to you arising out of or in connection with this engagement will be limited to the fee actually paid to us under it, save where the law does not permit such a limit, and neither of us will be liable to the other for indirect or consequential loss.
Governing Law

This letter, together with the signature page that accompanies it, constitutes the entire agreement between us in respect of this engagement, supersedes any prior discussion or understanding, and may be varied only by a writing signed by both of us. It will be governed by and construed in accordance with the law of the state in which our firm maintains its principal office, and each of us submits to the courts of that state in respect of any dispute arising under it.

If the terms set out above match your understanding of the assignment, I would ask you to sign and date the enclosed copy and return it to me, upon which we will confirm the commencement and begin. If any part of it warrants a conversation first, tell me and I will make the time this week to talk it through before you sign. I am Julie Ramsey, and I look forward to working with you and your people at {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}}.
Sincerely,

To: Matthew Parrish
From: Pamela Miller, Research Associate
Re: Back-Office Automation for {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} -- kickoff and workplan

The test of this engagement is whether {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} can run its own back office with less hand work and more confidence in the numbers once we have gone, not whether we produce a tidy map of the current state, and I am setting the workplan down now so the two of us start from one account of it rather than two. Our sponsor on the client side is Mark Villegas, their Chief Financial Officer, and he has been direct that the work is worth doing only if his own staff can operate the result without us in the room. Work begins on {{fact:f:E-2021-001.start}}, and the assignment is scoped to run about four months, which gives us room to understand the processes properly before we commit to which of them to automate first.
How the work splits

items: 1. Map the current processes. I will follow each of the main back-office routines end to end, from invoice receipt through reconciliation and close, and record where a step is done by hand only because it always has been.

2. Benchmark the cost and effort. Matthew Parrish will assemble the outside reference points, how comparable finance functions handle the same work and at what cost, so we can judge which processes at {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} are run well and which are merely run.

3. Rank the automation candidates. Together we will weigh each process by the effort it consumes against the difficulty of automating it, so the sequence we recommend begins where the return is surest.
4. Draft the automation design. Once the ranking holds, we set out how the leading processes would be redesigned, described in terms of what the change asks the client's staff to do differently.

blocks.text: These are not four tasks to run at once. The process map has to be right before the benchmarking means anything, and the ranking is only as sound as the map and the benchmarks beneath it. A design built on a process we have not actually watched tends to come apart the first time it meets a real invoice, so we hold to this order even when the client would like to see a recommendation sooner.
The opening weeks

Three things need to close in the first fortnight. I will have the list of back-office processes and their owners confirmed with the client by the end of the first week, so that we are studying the real routines and not an org chart's version of them. Matthew Parrish should have his first benchmark sources in hand by then, kept to the processes we already know are large, so we are not waiting on a wide search before we can begin. And I would like the two of us to walk through the current-state map together before the first client working session, so we arrive with one reading of it rather than two. If you can see a conflict in your first two weeks, tell me now, while the client dates are still open.
Hi Mark,

The process map for {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} is taking shape, and the one thing that would keep it moving is a fuller cut of the transaction detail behind your monthly close. I have the main routines sketched from what your team sent over, and Matthew Parrish is now setting the volumes against comparable finance functions, which is where the first real gaps in what we can see are showing up.

Two things from your side would help the cost work along: read access to the accounts-payable and reconciliation detail for the last full year, so we can see the effort by process rather than by department, and half an hour with whoever owns the monthly close, so that I am confirming from a short conversation what I would otherwise have to infer from the file. I know the timing is tight on your end, Mark Villegas, and I have kept the list as short as the work allows.

If any of that needs a sign-off on your side, point me at the right person and I will make the request directly rather than put it back on your desk; otherwise send whatever is easiest straight to me, Pamela Miller, and I will get it to the team the same day and keep this thread as the running record.
Regards
Working Session -- Back-Office Automation for {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}}

The session settled the order of the work for the next month: we will take the three back-office processes that consume the most staff time first, the payables handling, the account reconciliations, and the monthly reporting pack, and leave the smaller routines for a later pass, because that is where the process map shows the effort and the strongest case for automation both sit. The discussion below, and the actions at the end, all follow from that choice.
Present
Where the process map landed

Pamela Miller walked the group through the current-state map. Each of the three lead processes is now recorded end to end, from the point at which a document arrives to the point at which its entry is closed, with the manual steps marked and timed. Two steps that the client had treated as a single reconciliation turned out to be two separate checks, run by different people against different systems, which matters because we had been about to benchmark them as one. Pamela Miller also noted that a share of the payables volume never passes through the workflow system at all, so part of the map still rests on interviews rather than on system records.
What the benchmarks point to

On the three lead processes, the early read is that {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} carries more manual handling than comparable finance functions of its size, and that most of that handling clusters in a handful of steps a rule could take over without judgment being lost. I took the group through the outside reference points I have assembled so far, and Mark Villegas confirmed that the close has been staffed to its present shape for years without anyone asking whether the steps still need a person. We agreed that the payables handling and the reconciliations are the clearer early candidates, and that the reporting pack would follow once its inputs are cleaner.
What is still open

Two gaps remain before we can rank the candidates with any confidence. First, the payables volume that sits outside the workflow system has still to be pulled in from the invoice records, and until it is, the effort on that process is an estimate rather than a count. Second, the benchmarks cover only the first of the three lead processes in full, while the other two are in progress. Neither gap changes the direction of the work, but both bear on how firm a saving we can put against each process, and both are recorded here so the ranking is read as provisional and not as settled.
Action items

rows: Split the reconciliation step into its two underlying checks and re-time the affected processes
Complete the benchmarks for the remaining two lead processes against the outside reference points
Confirm which staff own each lead process and arrange the process walkthroughs
Pull the off-system payables volume from the invoice records so the effort is counted rather than estimated

blocks.text: The first step is the re-timed process map from Pamela Miller; the benchmarking and the ranking both wait on it, so that is the item to clear first.
Status Report -- Back-Office Automation for {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}}

The engagement is at roughly its midpoint and on plan: the back-office processes are mapped and benchmarked, we know which of them will repay automation and which will not, and the work is turning from diagnosis toward the design that will carry the savings. This report covers the period since the last one, sets out what is finished and what comes next, and names the risks I am watching. It was prepared by Pamela Miller, with the benchmarking led by Matthew Parrish.
Where things stand

The diagnosis is essentially complete. We now hold a current-state map of the back office at {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} that records each of the lead processes end to end, with the manual steps marked and timed, and a benchmarked view of how those processes compare with the way similar finance functions run them. On that basis we can say with reasonable confidence which processes will repay automation first and which are better left alone. The engagement remains within the fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2021-001.fee}} agreed at the outset, and nothing in the current plan calls for a change to it.
Finished this period

items: 1. Closed the current-state map of the three lead processes, the payables handling, the reconciliations, and the monthly reporting pack, and separated the reconciliation step that had been counted as one into the two checks it actually is.
2. Benchmarked the effort and cost of those processes against comparable finance functions, which between them account for the larger share of the manual work.
3. Pulled the payables volume that had been sitting outside the workflow system into the count, so the effort on that process now rests on records rather than on an estimate.
4. Ranked the lead processes by the return their automation would bring against the difficulty of achieving it, so the design starts where the case is surest.

blocks.text: Taken together, this closes the diagnostic work. We now know how the back office runs, where the manual effort concentrates, and which of it a rule could carry as well as a person. Matthew Parrish has kept the benchmarks tied to sources your own staff could check, and the process map is clean enough that one of your analysts could pick it up and follow it without a guide.
Planned for the coming weeks

items: 1. Draft the automation design for the two lead processes, setting out how each would be redesigned and what the change asks your staff to do differently.
2. Test the designs against real transactions, so we learn where they hold and where they break before they are recommended rather than after.
3. Sequence the remaining processes, so the design covers more than the two we are leading with.
4. Begin the adoption plan, describing what your own team would own and operate once we have gone.

blocks.text: The center of the next period is the design itself. Everything to this point has been about establishing what is true; the work now is deciding what to do with it, which means redesigning the leading processes, testing them against live cases, and preparing your people to run the result after the engagement has closed.
Risks I am watching

items: The share of back-office work that runs outside the main systems is larger than the client first expected, and bringing it into a designed process will take effort from your staff that competes with their day-to-day close.
The savings depend on your team operating the automated processes as designed after we leave, which is a matter of habit more than of analysis, and the adoption plan has to account for it.
One of the reporting-pack inputs is still being cleaned, so the design for that process rests for now on an assumption we are working to confirm from the source data.

blocks.text: None of these is off track, and each has an owner and a plan behind it. Matthew Parrish and I will bring the first automation designs to the next working session, and I will keep this report current so the picture you hold of the engagement matches the one we do.
